item.title: Hundreds of Drones Target Moscow on Final Day of Russian Elections
item.description:
Moscow and its surrounding region came under attack by hundreds of drones, the local authorities said on Sunday morning, killing two people and injuring 20.

About 1,600 drones heading toward the Moscow region were shot down, the Russian capital’s mayor, Sergei Sobyanin, said, including 450 that had been approaching the city. An oil refinery and a warehouse were struck in the attack.

The attack came on the final day of parliamentary, regional and local elections across Russia. Russian officials have repeatedly said they are holding these votes under attack, possibly an implicit criticism of Ukraine, which has not held elections since the start of Russia’s full-scale invasion in 2022 because martial law forbids them. President Vladimir V. Putin has repeatedly criticized Kyiv and President Volodymyr Zelensky for not holding a vote.

Mr. Zelensky posted on Facebook that the bombardment included the first use of a newly developed Ukrainian ballistic missile to strike inside Russia. That missile does not have the range to reach Moscow, according to its manufacturer, Fire Point, so would have been aimed elsewhere in Russia.

The night was deadlier in Ukraine, where seven people were killed in strikes in the Kyiv and Sumy regions, according to Ukrainian authorities. Air alerts were on and off all night though most of the country.

Moscow’s mayor said “a few drones” struck the Moscow oil refinery in Kapotnya, which had been taken out of commission by attacks in June. At the time, it was estimated that the repairs would last for six months. On Sunday, Mr. Sobyanin said the refinery had again been damaged.

In the neighborhood of Ramenskoye, a 21-story building caught fire, and 600 residents were evacuated, said Moscow’s regional governor, Andrei Vorobyov.

A warehouse in the Moscow region was also struck, though no casualties were reported. For months, Ukraine has been targeting warehouses in Russia with long-range strikes.

All four airports in the Moscow region introduced temporary restrictions at the time of the attacks, and more than 30 flights were grounded, according to the newspaper Kommersant.

On Saturday, Mr. Sobyanin reported that a total of 2,022 drones had flown toward the Moscow region over the preceding seven days, 186 of which were shot down as they approached Moscow. Most of the drones had been shot down while they were still far from the city.

President Trump said last Monday that Kyiv and Moscow had agreed to stop campaigns of pounding one another’s energy infrastructure but neither side has confirmed that an agreement had been reached. The attacks have continued through the week.

The outcome of the Russian elections looks to be a foregone conclusion: victory for the ruling party that supports Mr. Putin, because the Kremlin has engineered the vote to minimize competition.

Russians dread what may come after the Kremlin receives what most expect will be its desired result at the ballot box — whether that be another, albeit quieter, round of mobilization, more tax rises or more internet restrictions.

The country is already facing widespread fuel shortages because of Ukraine’s attacks on refineries. While fuel lines have become commonplace in the last few months, there were few on Saturday because not many fuel stations had any gas to sell. When they had something, it was low-quality gas or diesel.

In his statement on Facebook, Mr. Zelensky said the Ukrainians had struck with several types of domestically made drones and missiles created during the war in response to Russian missile attacks on Ukraine. These included Fury, FP-1 and Flamingo exploding drones, the Palianytsia cruise missile and the FP-7 Pelican ballistic missile, Mr. Zelensky said in the statement.

The Pelican missile is already in production in Ukraine, along with a larger, longer-range version expected to enter combat tests later this fall. The longer-range version, the FP-9, could reach Moscow.

item.title: Houthis Push to Expand Territory as Tensions With Saudi Arabia Rise
item.description:
The Iran-backed Houthi militia in Yemen was engaged in fierce battles against fighters backed by Saudi Arabia on Sunday, as the group steps up its push to expand its territory, according to local officials.

The ground fighting is the latest sign of how the war between Saudi Arabia and the Houthis that resumed in July is escalating. On Saturday, the armed group said it had launched missiles and drones at Riyadh, the Saudi capital, and at oil facilities, in retaliation for hundreds of Saudi airstrikes and other attacks inside Yemen.

On Sunday, battles were raging in al-Wazi’iyah, al-Madaribah and al-Arah, mountainous territory in the southwest of Yemen, according to Abdul Basit al-Baher, an army officer with the Saudi-backed government. If the Houthis gain control of the areas, they could cut off the city of Taiz from the southern capital of Aden and lay siege to Saudi-backed forces in Taiz, he added.

Fierce battles have also taken place in recent days around Kahboub, a mountainous territory that overlooks the Bab al-Mandab Strait, a choke point for international shipping, according to two other Yemeni officials. The waterway became a critical trade route for Saudi Arabia after Iran effectively blockaded the Strait of Hormuz in the Persian Gulf. The officials spoke on the condition of anonymity because they were not authorized to speak to the news media.

Saudi officials have not responded to repeated requests for comment on the war. The government has not acknowledged carrying out recent airstrikes in Yemen or responded to a Houthi claim that the group shot down a Saudi fighter jet last week.

In a statement about the attack on Riyadh, Maj. Gen. Turki al-Maliki, a spokesman for a Saudi-led military coalition in Yemen, said that it “holds the inherent right to take appropriate measures,” but provided no details.

One question hanging over Saudi Arabia’s deliberations is whether the United States, the kingdom’s most powerful ally, will increase military assistance against the Houthis, or become directly involved.

Saudi officials have been clear that the kingdom does not want to fight the Houthis alone. That is especially true because the earlier, yearslong military campaign that Saudi Arabia led against the group turned into a quagmire. The conflict damaged the kingdom’s reputation, strained its finances and contributed to the deaths of hundreds of thousands of Yemenis from violence, hunger and disease.

President Trump rebuffed an appeal this month by Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman of Saudi Arabia, the country’s de facto ruler, for increased military support to battle the Houthis, according to officials with knowledge of the conversations.

Around the same time, the Houthis seized control of Yemen’s entire Red Sea coastline, giving the group greater control over shipping in the waterway.

The Houthis and Yemeni government forces have been at war since 2014, when the Houthis seized the country’s capital, Sanaa. Soon after, a Saudi-led military coalition began a bombing campaign to try to restore the government to power, plunging the impoverished nation into a devastating conflict. A fragile truce, reached in 2022, has unraveled amid the U.S.-Israeli war with Iran.

The fighting reignited in July after the Houthis accused Saudi Arabia of bombing Sanaa’s airport. The Saudi-backed government claimed responsibility for the attack, saying it was trying to prevent an Iranian aircraft from landing.

Soon after, the Houthis declared a blockade on Saudi shipping in the Red Sea.

For years, Yemen has been effectively divided into two states, with the Houthis in control of much of the north and the south nominally under the authority of an internationally recognized government, which depends heavily on Saudi Arabia for financial and military support.

The militia, however, has increasingly referred to itself as the legitimate government of Yemen.

Last week, Mohammed al-Bukhaiti, a Houthi political official, said in an interview that the group “assures everyone that it is concerned with liberating every inch of Yemeni territory.” He dismissed Yemeni government officials as “Saudi mercenaries.”

Shuaib Almosawa contributed reporting from Sanaa, Yemen and Saeed Al-Batati contributed reporting from al-Mukalla, Yemen.

item.title: Let’s Talk Climate
item.description:
I’m in New York City this week, along with dozens of world leaders who have come for their annual gathering at the United Nations. They have a lot to talk about — wars, an oil shock, the risks of A.I., a shifting world order. One thing that looks set to be less of a talking point? Climate change.

It’s striking. Twenty years ago, “An Inconvenient Truth” hit movie theaters. Eight years ago, Fridays for Future was a global youth movement. The next year, Green parties all over Europe made historic gains. Today extreme weather has turned climate change from an abstract future threat into a real and present danger. And yet, the climate feels much less central to the political agenda.

But I’m going to a place where the climate will be front and center. The New York Times is holding its Climate Forward conference. My colleague David Gelles, who writes the Climate Forward newsletter, is hosting. I talked to David about what to expect.

David, why are world leaders so quiet on climate change when it’s been producing a steady stream of headline news this year?

I think there are three reasons. The first is that there’s a lot going on, right? Whether it’s war or A.I. or tariffs, the world is just consumed by a host of other crises.

The second reason is President Trump. His administration has dismissed the threat of climate change and is working to promote fossil fuels, reduce environmental regulations and stymie America’s adoption of renewable technologies. The rest of the world may be moving in a different direction, but they’re, at some level, captive to the American narrative, just by virtue of America’s power in the world.

The final reason is I think many leaders still have a hard time talking about climate. It’s still really hard to address. The actual solutions that are necessary to meaningfully slow down global warming require whole-cloth changes to our economies and energy systems that no one country alone can accomplish.

How are we doing fighting climate change? What’s the state of play?

It’s not great. Just a couple of years ago, people involved in climate policy were using the phrase “keep 1.5 alive.” That number referred to 1.5 degrees Celsius, which is the threshold above preindustrial temperatures that scientists warned would be very risky to cross. Well, we’re already at 1.5 today, and every indication suggests that the planet is on track to warm somewhere between two and three degrees Celsius above preindustrial levels. A lot of that warming is going to happen in the coming decades and century.

Now, there is real positive momentum happening on the ground, if you know where to look. Major economies like China are turbocharging their adoption of renewables. It’s happening in less developed countries like Pakistan too, which is adopting things like e-scooters. So there’s progress. But even when that progress is happening on a large scale, it’s still a drop in the bucket. We’ve got a long way to go.

You’re based in America, where, as you noted, the administration dismisses climate change and has made a strategic decision to double down on fossil fuels. Can the world combat climate change without the United States?

I think the world can’t do this without the U.S., but not just because the U.S. is a major emitter. It’s because U.S. policy and precedent and industry all matter for the rest of the world’s ability to scale these technologies.

Take natural gas. The Trump administration is using natural gas exports as a diplomatic tool. They’re actively encouraging countries around the world to hasten their adoption of natural gas, which is a major pollutant and is warming the planet. So what’s happening now in the United States isn’t just about domestic policy. It’s also making it much harder for the rest of the world to move quickly to address this issue.

What are some of the highlights of this year’s Climate Forward event? (Which, by the way, people will be able to livestream with no paywall.)

Well, as discussed, if you want to understand what’s happening globally on climate, you have to understand what’s happening in the United States. And on Wednesday, we’re going to have a collection of politicians, executives and activists who are going to give a comprehensive overview of the main issues driving the debate in the U.S. right now. That includes Chris Wright, the U.S. energy secretary, who will be able to speak to the administration’s policies. We’ll have the C.E.O.s of a bunch of very consequential energy and mining companies give you the industry perspective as well. You, Katrin, are speaking with Gerard Barron, for instance, who runs a deep-sea mining company.

But we’ll also have Jane Fonda, the actor and activist who’s now campaigning against petrochemical development on the Gulf Coast. We’ll have people on different sides of the A.I. debate — Josh Parker, who leads sustainability at Nvidia, and Erin Brockovich, who is campaigning against data centers. And we’ll have scientists like Kate Marvel.

Final question. David, you’ve covered climate change for many years. It’s a frustrating and difficult subject. Are you still excited about it? What makes you stick with it?

The reason I took on this beat is because I was looking for a story that would be able to occupy me for the rest of my life. And climate change is that story.

We are literally not going to solve this problem in my lifetime. I certainly hope we make progress, for the sake of preventing additional disasters and biodiversity and ecosystem loss. At the same time, I recognize the modern world is built on technologies that are exacerbating these problems. And so figuring out that puzzle is endlessly compelling. This is the greatest collective action problem in the history of humanity. And we’ve got to figure it out because if we don’t, we’re going to have a much harder time surviving on this planet.

As Xi Jinping arrives in the U.S. this week for a state visit, China’s advances in artificial intelligence will be in the air. What will be less discussed is that he is also the leader of an economy in its worst shape in decades.

Economists in China, even those closest to the state, have openly warned that the government is pouring too many resources into a technology that creates relatively few jobs, while doing too little to improve the broader economy. The Chinese A.I.-centered allocation of resources could prove costly to ordinary people’s livelihoods and the country’s economic future, they say.

Germany’s chancellor, Friedrich Merz, vowed to remain in the job after his party performed poorly in two state elections. “It is a disaster,” he said after the polls closed.

The Houthi militia in Yemen engaged in fierce battles against fighters backed by Saudi Arabia, a day after it said it had launched missiles and drones at Riyadh.

Ukraine attacked the Moscow region with hundreds of drones on the final day of elections across Russia.

An Israeli man was shot and killed in the occupied West Bank, according to Israeli authorities, who said they had detained a Palestinian suspect.

Trump said his planned arch in Washington would be built to host “large numbers of drones,” snipers and ammunition.

Ed Sheeran acknowledged “mistakes” and apologized to fans after his tour was roiled by the removal of Macklemore over pro-Palestinian comments.

“La Bola Negra,” a Spanish epic about the intertwined lives of three gay men over decades, won the top prize at the Toronto International Film Festival.

Watch our chief fashion critic recap New York Fashion Week.

The most clicked link in your newsletter on Friday was about an athlete who soiled herself during a high-endurance race.

The tilcayo is the first living feline species added to the cat family tree since 1923. It’s smaller than a house cat and lives in the cloud forests of the Andes in Bolivia. DNA analysis revealed that it split from its closest cat relatives more than a million years ago.

The Philippines is one of many countries trying to deal with energy shocks from the wars in Ukraine and the Middle East. The government is exploring nuclear power options. One proposal is to revive a plant in Bataan that was completed 42 years ago but never switched on.

Bringing it to life is not impossible, but it is a big and expensive ask, experts say. The project has divided Filipinos. Read more and take a look inside the 1970s power plant.

In Xalapa, the capital of Veracruz State, a joke among friends has grown into an annual melon race and a contest for the city’s most handsome melon.​

It started more than two decades ago when friends filmed melons rolling down a cobblestone bridge. Now, there are nine heats with 25 melons each — and a beauty contest. Read more and decide which melon you find most attractive.

Visit: It may look like a spaceship, but that building is the new Lucas Museum of Narrative Art.

Read: Michael Moritz’s memoir, “Ausländer,” explores his Jewish family’s history.

Watch: The documentary “You Had To Be There” revisits the “Godspell” production that started several now-legendary comedy careers.

Explore: Here’s how to spend 36 hours in Lake Como.

Mild white fish becomes deeply savory in this quick one-pot meal inspired by the Vietnamese dish cá kho tộ. The sauce is fantastic with tofu, chicken, meat, vegetables and seafood. Just make sure you have plenty of rice to soak it up.

Which town is this?

Saint-Pierre, Saint Pierre and Miquelon

Qaqortoq, Greenland

Lunenburg, Nova Scotia

Percé, Québec

Here are today’s Spelling Bee, Mini Crossword, Wordle and Sudoku. Find all our games here.

That’s it for today. See you tomorrow! — Katrin

We welcome your feedback. Send us your suggestions at theworld@nytimes.com.

item.title: On a Dot of France Off Canada, Carney and Macron Talk Partnership
item.description:
As part of Canada’s effort to knit closer ties with Europe, Prime Minister Mark Carney flew on Sunday to a French island just a ferry ride off Canada’s Newfoundland coast to meet with France’s president, Emmanuel Macron.

The brief encounter on St. Pierre, part of a speck of French territory in North America, comes before the opening of the United Nations General Assembly and days after the European Union invited Canada to become an “associate member.”

Neither leader offered any further details about that offer. (Associate membership is not a category that currently exists in the bloc.) But both men made it clear that the idea is a response to the breakdown in each’s formerly close relations with the United States, brought on by President Trump. Neither Mr. Macron nor Mr. Carney mentioned the president by name.

Instead, Mr. Macron highlighted interests that France and Canada share that the Trump administration rejects.

“We both believe that our two countries are strong, independent nations that wish to remain that way,” Mr. Macron said in a speech following a private meeting. “We both believe in democracy, in the respect for international law, and for free and fair trade, science on which rests our decisions, and of course, the strategic issues around which we work.”

Mr. Carney, for his part, said that “the time has come to tighten our ties.”

“Canada and Europe will build an alliance for the future that will strengthen our collective resilience so we can live the lives we choose, based on the values that we share across Fortune Bay,” he added, referring to the body of water that separates St. Pierre from Canada’s Newfoundland.

Last week Mr. Trump said that a closer relationship between Canada and Europe could be perceived as “a hostile act.”

Mr. Trump has expanded his trade war with Canada by imposing additional 50 percent tariffs on $20 billion of Canadian exports and by banning the entry of some Canadian products. The moves followed the collapse of trade talks between the countries. Mr. Carney has attributed the failure to unacceptable demands from the United States, while Trump administration officials blamed Canada for making last-minute demands.

The president has also continued his social media slights against Canada, including recent posts of maps that overlaid the American flag on Canada, as well as on St. Pierre and the neighboring French island of Miquelon.

In a speech to the European Union last week, Mr. Carney said that a stronger alliance with Europe would preserve Canada’s sovereignty and freedom amid a “ferocious storm.”

The only thing certain about the invitation for associate E.U. membership is that it cannot be full membership. Aside from the E.U.’s legal requirement that members must be in Europe, it would likely be impossible for Mr. Carney, or any other Canadian leader, to sell Canadians on the idea that the best way to protect their sovereignty from American aggression would be to give some of it up to Europe.

And some Europeans — as well as Mr. Carney — appear uncomfortable about using the word “member” at all to describe the new partnership.

Canada and Europe already have a free-trade agreement, so little would be likely to change there. Analysts speculate that the new relationship could align some regulations, make it easier for some people (likely students) to move between continents, or strengthen the ties of financial services across the ocean. Mr. Macron and Mr. Carney both mentioned working together on A.I.

After quickly returning to Ottawa Mr. Carney met in Ottawa with Prime Minister Jonas Gahr Store of Norway, a country with expertise on special arrangements with the E.U.

After Norwegians twice rejected joining Europe in referendums, it is now part of the European Economic Area. That leaves Norway subject to many European regulations, without having any say in how they are implemented. It also contributes money to E.U. funds intended to equalize economic and social programs throughout the continent. Norwegians can travel passport free to E.U. countries.

Afterward, the two men had little to say to reporters regarding any discussion they may have had about Canada joining Europe. Instead they focused on the growing connections between Canada and Norway, which Mr. Carney visited in March. In what Mr. Carney described as Canada’s largest military procurement in its history, his government said in July that it will buy a fleet of submarines from a Norwegian-German joint venture.

When asked by a reporter if Mr. Trump could also see a closer Norwegian-Canadian relationship as a “hostile act,” Mr. Carney said that “deeper ties between NATO allies makes those NATO allies stronger, makes NATO stronger and helps to achieve the common goals of all NATO members very much, the United States included.”

item.title: One Issue That Could Upend Fragile U.S.-China Ties: Taiwan Arms
item.description:
For China’s leader, Xi Jinping, one important goal of his meeting with President Trump this week may be persuading him to keep delaying $14 billion in proposed U.S. arms sales to Taiwan.

China has long claimed the self-governed island of Taiwan as its territory, and Taipei has relied on American military power to counter military threats from Beijing. When they last met, Mr. Xi warned Mr. Trump that mishandling tensions over Taiwan could be “extremely dangerous” for the United States and China, a reminder of the risk of crisis between two nuclear-armed powers.

“There’s only one issue that could cause relations between both sides to break down completely or erupt in conflict, and that is Taiwan,” said Xin Qiang, the director of the Center for Taiwan Studies at Fudan University in Shanghai.

“Demanding a continued delay in any arms sales may be the most critical issue,” he said.

Mr. Trump has described the arms sale plan as a source of leverage with China. After his May summit with Mr. Xi in Beijing, Mr. Trump said he had discussed the deal with the Chinese leader. “It’s a very good negotiating chip for us, frankly,” he said then.

Mr. Trump has since held off approving the package of missiles, anti-drone weaponry and air-defense systems. His administration has also muted public references to Taiwan: Officials, including Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth, have conspicuously avoided mentioning Taiwan in speeches.

For Beijing, Mr. Trump’s willingness to delay arms sales is already a gain. In Washington, Mr. Xi could hint at potential costs if Mr. Trump approves the sale, including more restrictions on Chinese rare earth exports. Mr. Xi could also signal that he might skip the Group of 20 summit in Miami in December, which Mr. Trump will preside over.

Mr. Trump, for his part, may want China to increase pressure on Iran to reopen the Strait of Hormuz, the critical waterway for global oil and gas supplies that Iran has effectively blocked since the war began in February.

“I think in Beijing we saw the opening move in what will be a sophisticated play to get the Trump administration to reduce support for Taiwan,” said David Sacks, a fellow at the Council on Foreign Relations who studies U.S. relations with Taiwan and China. “Xi will use his meetings with Trump in Washington to continue to implement this strategy.”

Delayed arms sales are a political headache for Taiwan’s president, Lai Ching-te. He has promoted increased military spending and purchases of American weapons, in part to meet the Trump administration’s own demands that partners invest more in their defense. Mr. Trump’s stalling could make it harder for Mr. Lai to defend his agenda.

Longer delays could drag on the island’s military goals, partly by pushing Taiwan further back in the line for orders of scarce military hardware, some experts said.

“Ultimately, it’s a game of the Chinese trying to prolong this process as long as possible, with the idea being that if China can make gains faster than Taiwan can acquire capabilities, then the balance continues to tilt in Beijing’s favor,” said Ryan Hass, a former director for China at the National Security Council and a senior fellow at the Brookings Institution.

Some experts said they expected Mr. Trump to keep holding off approval of any arms sales for Taiwan until at least late this year. Others said the green light for some weapons could come sooner. Both Republicans and Democrats in Congress are likely to raise pressure on the administration to approve the proposed arms sales after the summit, Mr. Sacks said.

The arms issue has highlighted Taiwan’s struggles to keep Mr. Trump onside. Taiwan does not have formal diplomatic relations with the United States, and Mr. Trump’s highly personalized, freewheeling style makes it more difficult for Taiwan to understand and shape U.S. decision-making, experts say.

“With an administration that is so top-down, I think that is hindering the Taiwanese ability to get a really good sense of what’s going on and the ability to help shape and influence that,” said Laura Rosenberger, a former Biden administration official who oversaw U.S. policies on China and Taiwan.

In his first term, Mr. Trump signed off on about $18 billion of arms sales to Taiwan, and hawkish members of his government focused on Beijing as a long-term threat. But in his second term, Mr. Trump has emphasized pragmatic ties with China, largely retreating from a trade war after Beijing strangled exports of rare earths that are crucial for smartphones and advanced technology.

Taiwan has sought to maintain influence by cultivating Mr. Trump’s inner circle, hiring lobbyists and arranging visits to the island for prominent supporters of the president.

But some Taiwanese officials who have traveled to the United States have also been told by Trump administration officials to curtail their visits to research groups in Washington, said Mr. Hass at the Brookings Institution.

“All of this just betrays a clear preference by President Trump to ensure Taiwan does not become an obstacle to his ambitions as it relates to China,” he said.

Still, Taiwan’s security relationship with the United States remains robust. Officials and experts say working ties between government departments have remained steady, even deepened.

During Taiwan’s annual Han Kuang military exercises last month, American advisers were more visible than in past years. At a recent briefing with reporters, Taiwan’s defense minister, Wellington Koo, spoke coyly of growing numbers of “American English teachers,” a euphemism for the U.S. military advisers whose presence rankles Beijing.

“Our friends in the U.S. government understand how important continued arms sales are for Taiwan’s defense,” Chen Ming-chi, a deputy minister in Taiwan’s foreign ministry who handles relations with the United States, said in an interview.

Taiwan’s importance as an American trading partner has also grown sharply; this year it surpassed China as the third biggest source of U.S. imports, behind Mexico and Canada, according to U.S. figures. The bulk of those imports are semiconductors and other high-tech equipment sustaining the artificial intelligence boom in the United States. Taiwanese officials hope this growth will ultimately help entrench American support.

“We are probably the most cooperative partner in the whole world when it comes to tariffs and investment in the United States,” Mr. Chen said.

Mr. Trump often complains about Taiwan’s dominance in making advanced semiconductors, raising his long-held, and widely debunked, accusation that the island pilfered chip-making know-how from the United States. “They got stolen from us and they were brought to Taiwan,” Mr. Trump said last month in a radio interview.

But displacing Taiwan as a chief source of advanced chips is unlikely, even as Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Company, or TSMC, the main global chip maker, expands production in the United States, experts say. TSMC has said it will spend $265 billion on its plants in Arizona. But Taiwan’s dense networks of suppliers and engineering talent remains difficult to replicate.

“Building structural interdependence with our most critical ally provides the ultimate assurance for our national security,” said Jeremy Chih-Cheng Chang, the director of economic security studies at the Research Institute for Democracy, Society, and Emerging Technology in Taipei, which receives funding from the Taiwanese government.

“Presidents come and go," said Mr. Chang, “but Silicon Valley and Wall Street remain constant.”

item.title: Putin Reignited a Dispute With Japan. This Town Is Stuck in the Middle.
item.description:
The news traveled quickly on a paradisiacal summer day in Nemuro, a remote fishing town in northern Japan. President Vladimir V. Putin of Russia, in a show of strength, had made a surprise visit to a nearby chain of islands that both Russia and Japan claim.

At Nemuro’s City Hall, Mayor Masatoshi Ishigaki was concerned. For decades, the town’s residents have promoted Japan’s claims to the snow-capped island chain that Mr. Putin was visiting, with patriotic museums, billboards (“Give it back!”) and monuments.

But Nemuro, on the northern island of Hokkaido, also depends on Russia for trade and fishing rights, and Mr. Ishigaki worried any flare-up could hurt the economy.

“When friction arises between Japan and Russia, the pain is felt here immediately,” he said inside his office at City Hall, where the disputed islands loom in the distance on clear days.

The fight over the archipelago, known in Japan as the Northern Territories and in Russia as the southern Kuril Islands, has festered since 1945, when Moscow seized the territory from Japan in the final weeks of World War II. Japan has pushed Russia for years to relinquish control of at least two of four inhabited islands. But Moscow has resisted, and the two sides have yet to sign a peace treaty formally ending the war.

Now Mr. Putin has revived the issue — an effort, analysts say, to put pressure on Sanae Takaichi, Japan’s hawkish prime minister, and to rally nationalist sentiment in Russia.Mr. Putin has increased the frequency and scale of military exercises in the seas near Nemuro. He has said that Russia’s claims to the islands are a “reality” that has been “enshrined in international documents.” He has attacked Japan for maintaining economic sanctions on Russia that were imposed after his invasion of Ukraine in 2022. And he has encouraged criticism of Tokyo; Russia recently unveiled a statue showing a Soviet soldier smashing the chrysanthemum seal of Japan’s imperial family.

On his visit last month to the disputed islands, the first in his quarter-century rule, Mr. Putin ate caviar and toured a seafood-processing plant. He was shown on Russian state television meeting with adoring crowds under a bright sun; one woman told him “the weather is smiling on you.”

Ms. Takaichi has called Mr. Putin’s visit “absolutely unacceptable” and said he “hurt the feelings of the Japanese people.” Her government has protested a new world map that shows Russia and the disputed islands in the same shade of yellow.

Nowhere are the tensions more deeply felt than in Nemuro, a serene town of about 22,000 that is known for icy winters, kaleidoscopic sunrises and the bright-red spiny king crabs harvested on its shores.

Nemuro lies just a few miles from the southernmost part of the disputed islands, which are part of an archipelago stretching from the southern tip of the Kamchatka Peninsula in eastern Russia to Hokkaido at the top of Japan.

Like many rural Japanese towns, Nemuro has suffered from long-term demographic decline; its population is now about half of its peak of about 50,000 in the 1960s. Many young people have left for jobs and schools in Tokyo and other cities, as the economy has been hit by Russian-imposed limits on fishing for salmon and trout, and as trade has dwindled.

Russian sailors used to abound in Nemuro — so much so that the local schools still teach Russian, and stores cater to Russian visitors, who once came in search of refrigerators, ovens, bicycles, smartphones and televisions. Nemuro’s ports still display posters in fading Cyrillic type, including one that says: “Dear foreign sailors! Please practice safe navigation!”

But as relations between Japan and Russia have deteriorated in recent years, many Russians have stayed at home, hurting business at Nemuro’s restaurants, bars and seafood processors. For those who still come — hawking sea urchin, mackerel and kelp — it can be lonely.

“It feels like we’re the last of the Russians,” said Alexey Dudka, a sailor from the nearby Russian port town of Kholmsk, who was stopping in Nemuro for repairs on his ship. “It’s a ghost town now.”

Despite its links to Russia, Nemuro has long been on the front lines of Japan’s efforts to win back the disputed islands, roughly the size of the state of Delaware. The town is filled with nationalistic posters that proclaim, “The Northern Territories are a Japanese territory.” A museum shows ancient books and maps meant to prove Japan’s longstanding ties to the islands. Japan traces its claims to the islands to the 17th century.

The patriotic mission in Nemuro has traditionally been led by former residents of the islands from Japan, but their ranks are dwindling. There are now about 4,700 living former residents in Japan, down from about 17,000 who were expelled by the Soviet Union at the end of World War II. They have an average age of about 90.

Hiroshi Tokunou, 92, was 11 in 1945 when Soviet troops occupied the islands. After living and studying alongside the Soviets for a brief period, he and his relatives were sent to an internment camp, to make way for incoming Soviet families. In 1947, they were allowed to return to Hokkaido.

Mr. Tokunou said Mr. Putin “operates with a kind of cunning shrewdness,” adding that Japan should be firm in dealing with Russia. But, he said, “We also have to leave room for better relations in the future, for a rekindling down the line.” He said he was concerned the issue might fade if it is not taken up by Nemuro’s younger residents, who he worries have a “different way of thinking.”

Outside a local supermarket, Natsumi Nishita, 34, said it was “hard to get the same level of passion” as Nemuro’s elders about the dispute. Ms. Nishita, an English teacher at a cram school in Nemuro, said there were more important issues to worry about, like the economy.

“What Putin did was just a little thing that happened — a political appeal,” she said. “People here don’t think it’s a big deal.”

Mr. Ishigaki, the mayor of Nemuro, said he feels the islands are a missed opportunity for Japan; the local government estimates it could generate roughly $462 million each year in revenues from fisheries, seafood processing and other activities if it controlled the islands.

“We want to resolve this issue while we are still alive,” Mr. Ishigaki, 75, said.

Ms. Takaichi has refrained from penalizing Moscow over Mr. Putin’s visit, as Japan manages acute energy concerns because of the war in Iran. Japan imports about 10 percent of its liquefied natural gas from Russia.

Ms. Takaichi’s government had seemed interested in improving relations with Mr. Putin, restarting trade and cultural visits to Moscow earlier this year, despite some objections from European allies. But Mr. Putin’s visit has cast doubt on those efforts.

“Russia tends not to reciprocate when another side makes unilateral concessions,” said James D.J. Brown, a professor of political science at Temple University in Tokyo. “Instead, they double down on pressure.”

Every year, Nemuro holds ceremonies to remember ancestors buried on the islands. These rituals used to take place, with Moscow’s blessing, at cemeteries in the disputed territories.

But after Japan imposed sanctions on Russia in 2022, Mr. Putin suspended those visits and they are now performed at sea.

On a stormy morning this month, Taiko Kodama, 81, a retiree and activist who was born in the disputed territories, boarded a ferry to take part in a ceremony.

Aboard the boat, called the Puffin, she said a prayer for her parents and grandparents, and laid flowers in their memory. She keeps two black stones from the islands inside her purse to remember her homeland, which she fled in 1947, when she was 3. She said she still remembers the smell of kelp there.

“Our homes were taken from us unfairly,” she said. “We have to speak from our hearts.”

item.title: ‘Way Too Hot’: Britain’s Hospitals Were Not Built for 96-Degree Summers
item.description:
It was the fifth heat wave of the summer.

By late morning one day last month, the air inside Queen’s Medical Center in Nottingham, England, was thick and uncomfortable. Sweat glistened on the faces of staff members hurrying around the sprawling hospital. Patients tossed in their beds.

“It’s just getting to be way too hot; I am saying my prayers waiting for it to stop,” said Celia Burgess, 78, who was in a geriatric unit with two portable fans blowing in her direction. “I mean, they are trying, but it’s not much good. It’s these old hospitals.”

By late afternoon, temperatures in the central English city had reached more than 90 degrees Fahrenheit, and the following day, Nottingham reached 96 degrees. It was the hottest August day ever recorded in the city.

As average temperatures rise in Britain, so do fears that the country’s aging hospitals, built for a cooler climate, are ill equipped to cope. Few have air-conditioning, and many become alarmingly hot in the summer while also struggling with an influx of patients arriving with heat-related problems.

Those who use these facilities are already among society’s most vulnerable and most at risk from the heat, like older people, babies and children, and people with chronic illness.

This summer has been Britain’s hottest on record. As human-caused climate change accelerates, experts warn that nearly all National Health Service hospital buildings in England are at risk of overheating as summer temperatures grow more extreme, stretching Britain’s taxpayer-funded health system to a breaking point.

The pressures are twofold. More people are suffering from the effects of extreme heat, which strains emergency rooms, and hospital buildings are not designed to deal with the rising temperatures. During heat waves in May and June, there were 2,877 heat-associated deaths, according to preliminary data from the U.K. Health Security Agency — almost double the figure reported for last year.

At least five hospital groups in England declared critical incidents, an emergency status used when severe pressures make normal operations impossible. Queen’s Medical Center was among them. Its emergency room was overrun with patients in late June, and nonemergency care had to be curtailed. Other areas in the hospital, originally built in the 1960s, have had to be closed at times this summer amid overheating.

“These buildings were built for English winters. They weren’t built for the kind of summers we get now,” said Anthony May, the chief executive of Nottingham University Hospitals N.H.S. Trust, which oversees Queen’s Medical Center. “It seems climate change is catching up with us perhaps quicker than we can combat,” he added.

While the hospital has introduced measures to mitigate the heat, leaders are constrained, he said, by limited funding and the difficulty of retrofitting old buildings. About 90 percent of N.H.S. hospitals are at risk of overheating, according to a 2025 study from the U.K. Health Alliance on Climate Change. Most were built decades ago with architecture that prioritized retaining warmth for Britain’s cold, damp winters.

The new summer conditions are intensifying pressure on the N.H.S., which was already struggling after a period of sustained underinvestment following the 2008 financial crisis. A government effort called the New Hospital Program began in 2020, with plans to build dozens of new facilities across England by 2030, but delays have hindered it.

Hospital workers face “impossible and inhumane” conditions during the heat waves, the Royal College of Nursing, a union, warned last month.

“It’s unbearable,” said Ellie Brook, 27, a nurse and ward manager in a geriatric unit at Queen’s Medical Center. “You literally come away from the patients dripping in sweat.”

Her shared office space has no windows. The staff keeps the lights off and fans running to try to cool down. “Trying to get fans is like trying to get gold dust,” she said.

The U.K. Climate Change Committee, an independent body that advises the government, urged the government in a May report to invest in cooling in hospitals and other critical settings. It warned that increasingly extreme and frequent heat waves posed the greatest risk to health in Britain from climate change, and it predicted that excess deaths could double or even triple by 2050.

Hospitals are scrambling to adjust. In Nottingham, a hodgepodge of measures were in place last month, including fans, some portable air-conditioning units, and cool towels to ease patients’ discomfort. In the past year, tinted film was placed over some windows. A team has been examining data from a thermal imaging camera to identify parts of the hospital that grew particularly hot over the past five years. That will inform a plan for how to handle high temperatures in the longer term.

There are pockets of respite in the hospital. In the geriatric assessment unit, which opened in 2024, the effect of an air-conditioning system is clear the moment the doors open.

Elsewhere in Britain, new buildings show how hospitals could be designed to cope with the changing climate. The National Rehabilitation Center in Loughborough, which opened this month, is just 12 miles from Queen’s Medical Center, but feels worlds away. Costing about 107 million pounds (around $145 million), it was funded by the New Hospital Program and includes a modern system that regulates the temperature inside, including with heat pumps and solar panels.

For now, though, most patients and medical professionals are in structures more akin to Queen’s Medical Center. In the pediatric outpatient unit on the day we visited, Robyn Roy, 2, rested her head on her father’s chest, her face flushed, as a fan lifted strands of her hair. Robyn, who has Down syndrome, had undergone a routine operation that morning, and the temperature in the shared recovery room was rising.

Her father, Sam Roy, 27, said the staff was doing its best to keep everyone comfortable, but he was eager to get Robyn home.

“It can be hard to know if she is overheating, and she has breathing issues,” explained her mother, Courtney Roy, 26. Like many people with Down syndrome, Robyn has difficulty regulating her body temperature and has underlying heart issues, which make the heat even more worrying.

High temperatures can worsen chronic conditions, and children are already at higher risk from extreme heat, along with elderly people. April Rowan, 14, has a feeding tube, and it is hard for her to stay hydrated as a result of her chronic condition. Her mother, Gillian Rowan, said her concerns about her daughter’s health were compounded by the hot conditions in the hospital.

“It’s just horrendous,” she said. “You don’t get any airflow in here,” she added. “Everything just bakes.”
